title: Web framework: API design, versioning and GraphQL
description: Pagination (offset vs cursor), idempotency keys, status-code choice, API versioning and deprecation, and GraphQL with N+1 and DataLoader in Spring and Strawberry.
source: Spring Data JPA docs (Page/Slice/Pageable); RFC 9110 (HTTP semantics, conditional requests); RFC 9745 (Deprecation header) and RFC 8594 (Sunset); GraphQL specification (execution); Stripe idempotency docs; Spring for GraphQL docs (@BatchMapping); Strawberry docs; Use The Index, Luke (keyset pagination)
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.

questions.prompt: Match each API situation with the most appropriate HTTP status code.

left.text: Job queued; result will be available later
If-Match ETag no longer matches (optimistic locking)
DELETE sent to a read-only collection endpoint
Resource was removed on purpose and will not return

questions.explanation: 202 Accepted, 429 Too Many Requests (with Retry-After), 412 Precondition Failed, 405 Method Not Allowed (with Allow), 410 Gone. 409 is for state conflicts and 415 for an unsupported Content-Type.

questions.prompt: A Spring Data PageRequest.of(3, 20) is used (page index is zero-based). How many rows does the database skip with OFFSET?
questions.explanation: offset = page x size = 3 x 20 = 60, i.e. the 4th page. Pages in Spring Data start at 0, a common off-by-one trap.

questions.prompt: A GraphQL query lists 25 books and resolves author for each book. Each author resolver does its own SELECT, and the books list itself is one SELECT. How many SQL statements run in total?
questions.explanation: 1 for the list plus 25 (one per book) is the N+1 problem. With a DataLoader or @BatchMapping the 25 author lookups collapse into one, giving 2.

questions.prompt: Table posts(id, created_at, title). Write SQL that returns the next page, newest first, after the cursor (:last_created_at, :last_id). Fetch 21 rows (page size 20 plus one to detect a next page) with a deterministic tiebreaker.

checks.label: orders by created_at DESC, id DESC
filters with a keyset condition on (created_at, id)

questions.model:
SELECT id, created_at, title FROM posts
WHERE (created_at, id) < (:last_created_at, :last_id)
ORDER BY created_at DESC, id DESC
LIMIT 21;
questions.explanation: Keyset (cursor) pagination is stable under inserts and uses an index on (created_at, id). The expanded form created_at < :c OR (created_at = :c AND id < :i) is equally valid.

questions.prompt: Write a FastAPI POST /payments handler pay(body: PaymentIn, idempotency_key: str = Header(...)). A module-level dict store maps keys to earlier results: if the key was seen return the stored result, otherwise call charge(body), save it under the key, and return it.

checks.label: returns the stored result for a repeated key
saves the new result under the key

questions.explanation: In production the store is Redis or a DB table with a unique constraint on the key, and the check-and-save must be atomic (SET NX or INSERT ... ON CONFLICT), otherwise two concurrent retries both charge. Also store a hash of the body to reject a reused key with a different payload.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Offset pagination (LIMIT 20 OFFSET 100000) gets slower the deeper the client pages.
questions.reason: The database must walk past and discard all skipped rows before returning the page.

whys.a: Correct: cost grows with the offset, which is why cursor/keyset pagination is preferred for feeds.

questions.explanation: Deep offsets are O(offset). Offsets also drift when rows are inserted or deleted between requests.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Cursor pagination returns consistent pages while new rows are inserted during paging.
questions.reason: Cursors are usually encoded as opaque base64 tokens.

whys.a: Wrong: encoding is cosmetic and does not provide stability.
whys.b: Correct: stability comes from anchoring on a key value (not a row count); opaque encoding is a true but unrelated API-design choice.

questions.explanation: Opaque cursors let you change the underlying sort keys without breaking clients.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.reason: HTTP POST is idempotent by specification, so retrying it is always safe.

whys.c: Correct: A is true (repeated PUT leaves the same state), R is false; POST is not idempotent, hence Idempotency-Key.

questions.explanation: Safe methods: GET, HEAD, OPTIONS. Idempotent: those plus PUT and DELETE. POST and PATCH are not guaranteed idempotent.

questions.prompt: Judge the assertion and the reason.
questions.assertion: Returning Page<T> from a Spring Data repository avoids a separate COUNT query.
questions.reason: Slice<T> avoids the count query by fetching one extra row to learn whether a next page exists.

whys.d: Correct: Page<T> issues a count to know totals; Slice<T> skips it.

questions.explanation: Use Slice (or keyset) for infinite scroll and when the count is expensive.

questions.prompt: Select all that apply: which changes are backward compatible for existing JSON clients of v1?

options.text: Adding an optional field to a response.

options.why: Existing callers never use it, so nothing breaks.

options.text: Adding an optional query parameter with a default.
Renaming a response field from fullName to name.
options.why: Old clients that read fullName break.

options.text: Changing id from number to string.
options.why: Typed clients fail to parse it.

options.text: Making a previously optional request field required.

questions.explanation: Additive changes are safe; renames, type changes, removals and tightened validation are breaking and need a new version or a deprecation period.

questions.prompt: Using FastAPI APIRouter, create routers with the prefixes /v1 and /v2, add a GET /users route to v1 marked deprecated, and mount both routers on app.
questions.starter:
from fastapi import FastAPI, APIRouter
app = FastAPI()
questions.model:
v1 = APIRouter(prefix="/v1")
v2 = APIRouter(prefix="/v2")

@v1.get("/users", deprecated=True)
def users_v1():
    return []

app.include_router(v1)
app.include_router(v2)
questions.explanation: Verified: deprecated=True shows up in the generated OpenAPI. In Spring the same idea is @RequestMapping("/api/v1/users") per controller.

questions.prompt: Fill in the HTTP deprecation vocabulary.
questions.text: A server announces an endpoint is deprecated with the {1} response header (RFC 9745), gives the date it will stop working in {2} (RFC 8594), and can point to migration docs using a {3} header with rel values.
questions.explanation: Retry-After is for 429/503 and Warning is an obsolete caching header. Send these headers on old versions and log who still calls them before removal.

questions.prompt: In a Spring for GraphQL @Controller, write a batch resolver for the author field of Book: method author takes List<Book> books and returns Map<Book, Author>, loading all authors with one call authorRepo.findAllById(ids) instead of one query per book.

checks.label: takes List<Book> and returns Map<Book, Author>
loads authors in bulk with findAllById (or findByIdIn)

questions.explanation: @BatchMapping wraps a DataLoader so the framework batches all author lookups for one request. A hand-registered DataLoader (as in Strawberry's strawberry.dataloader.DataLoader) is the equivalent in Python.

questions.prompt: Using Strawberry, define a GraphQL type Book with a title: str field, a Query type with a field books returning list[Book], and build a schema.
questions.explanation: Mount it with strawberry.fastapi.GraphQLRouter(schema). For N+1 use strawberry.dataloader.DataLoader with a batch load function.

questions.prompt: A GraphQL query asks for books and each book's author. The author resolver throws for one book. What does a typical HTTP GraphQL server return?

options.text: HTTP 200 with partial data and an errors array.
options.why: GraphQL reports field errors in the body; the transport still succeeded.

options.text: HTTP 500 with an empty body, because the resolver crashed the request.
options.why: Field-level exceptions are caught by the engine and reported in errors.
GraphQL has a single endpoint; status codes do not map to fields.

options.text: HTTP 422 with a detail list like FastAPI REST.
options.why: That format belongs to FastAPI request validation, not GraphQL execution.

questions.explanation: Monitoring on status codes alone misses GraphQL failures; inspect the errors array.

questions.prompt: A GraphQL request contains three top-level mutation fields, m1, m2 and m3, and each resolver waits 100 ms on I/O. A spec-compliant server runs them one after another. Roughly how many milliseconds does the whole operation take?
questions.explanation: The GraphQL specification requires top-level mutation fields to execute serially, so 3 x 100 = 300 ms. Top-level query fields may run in parallel (about 100 ms). Serial order is what makes 'create then use' mutation lists predictable, and there is no rollback across them.

questions.prompt: A client re-requests GET /products/7 with If-None-Match set to the ETag it stored earlier, and the product has not changed. Which response is correct?

options.text: 304 Not Modified with no body; the client reuses its cached copy.
options.why: Correct: a matching If-None-Match on a GET gives 304, saving the transfer of the body.

options.text: 412 Precondition Failed, because the client sent a precondition header at all.
options.why: 412 is for If-Match style preconditions on unsafe requests; a matching If-None-Match on GET gives 304.

options.text: 204 No Content, because nothing changed since the last request.
options.why: 204 means success with an intentionally empty body, but it does not tell the client its cache is valid.

options.text: 200 OK with the full body again, since validators are only a hint meant for proxies.
options.why: A server that honours validators answers 304; sending 200 would waste the bandwidth ETags exist to save.

questions.explanation: Conditional GET: If-None-Match + ETag gives 304 when unchanged. The mirror image for writes is If-Match, where a mismatch yields 412 and enables optimistic concurrency over HTTP.
